title: Goanna

names.gloss: sand goanna. Only old people are allowed to eat it.
names.note: The food rule is part of the dictionary entry.

identification.basis: The dictionary distinguishes the goannas by country and colour, not by species. Kalajarr 'scrub goanna' and walkarr 'black scrub goanna' are most likely forms of the lace monitor (Varanus varius), the big goanna of the rainforest and forest. Jadi 'sand goanna' is most likely Gould's sand goanna (Varanus gouldii) or the similar yellow-spotted goanna (V. panoptes) of dry, sandy country. Which exact species each word covers is not settled.

summary: Kuku Yalanji names three goannas: **[kalajarr](word:kalajarr)**, the scrub goanna; **[walkarr](word:walkarr)**, the black scrub goanna; and **[jadi](word:jadi)**, the sand goanna. Of jadi the dictionary says plainly: 'Only old people are allowed to eat it' [ref:hershberger1982]. Roth called goannas 'iguanas'. He recorded them [speared](entry:spear-and-woomera) in the open or dug out of hollow logs and burrows [ref:roth1901]. On the Bloomfield River he noted that old men could set food restrictions and sometimes relaxed them for young men when food was scarce [ref:roth1908]. The lace monitor of the forests grows to about 1.5 m and is a skilled tree-climber [ref:wtma-monitors]. Sand goannas dig deep burrows in dry country [ref:nesp-sandgoanna]. Which goannas you meet depends on the place: see each place below.

sections.heading: Names
sections.body: The dictionary gives **[kalajarr](word:kalajarr)** 'scrub goanna', **[walkarr](word:walkarr)** 'black scrub goanna' and **[jadi](word:jadi)** 'sand goanna. Only old people are allowed to eat it' [ref:hershberger1982]. It also gives *[wangku](word:wangku)*, 'small tree or wood goanna' [ref:hershberger1982]. Roth, writing in English, called all of these animals 'iguanas', the old Queensland bush word for goannas [ref:roth1901].

sections.heading: Description
sections.body:
**Lace monitor** (probably *[kalajarr](word:kalajarr)* and *[walkarr](word:walkarr)*). A big goanna, up to about one and a half metres long. It spends much of its time in trees and is a major raider of birds' nests. It also eats reptiles, small mammals, large insects, carrion and food scraps. Lace monitors sometimes saunter through campgrounds looking for food, but if startled they run straight up the nearest tree [ref:wtma-monitors].

**Sand goanna** (probably *[jadi](word:jadi)*). A large goanna, well over a metre long, light yellow to blackish-brown with dense dark speckles and pale spots. A dark stripe runs back from the eye, and the tail is banded with a pale yellow tip [ref:nesp-sandgoanna]. It digs large burrows for shelter and also uses rock crevices, hollow logs and thick litter. It eats other animals, alive or dead [ref:nesp-sandgoanna]. Trackers read its footprints and tail mark, its diggings and its burrow entrances [ref:nesp-sandgoanna].

sections.heading: Where they live
sections.body:
The 'scrub' goannas belong to the forest. The lace monitor is the big monitor of the Wet Tropics, at home on the ground and in the trees [ref:wtma-monitors].

The sand goanna is an animal of drier, sandier country. It lives across many habitats of arid and semi-arid Australia, likes warm places with sandy, low-clay soils, and digs large burrows [ref:nesp-sandgoanna].

sections.heading: Uses
sections.body:
**Food.** Goannas were good meat, and Roth recorded them taken across North Queensland [ref:roth1901]. Goanna fat had its own uses; see the upper Mitchell below.

**Food rules.** The rule for **[jadi](word:jadi)** is printed in the dictionary: 'Only old people are allowed to eat it' [ref:hershberger1982]. The dictionary records the same rule for a [small freshwater eel](entry:eels), *[mawul](word:mawul)*, and for the stingray, *[yawu](word:yawu)*, 'long ago' [ref:hershberger1982]. Kuku Yalanji has words for these restrictions, *[jalbayn](word:jalbayn)* 'food taboo' and *[jabul](word:jabul)* 'taboo' [ref:hershberger1982]. On the Bloomfield, Roth (who wrote the word *tcha-bul*) recorded that food restrictions were 'often relaxed by some of the very old men in favour of the young males when food happens to be extra scarce'. More generally, he noted that old men could place a ban on any food they wished to keep for themselves when it was scarce [ref:roth1908]. Among the lower Tully River people, the 'iguana' was one of the land foods forbidden to young people [ref:roth1908].

sections.heading: How they were hunted and cooked
sections.body:
Roth's general account is that goannas 'are [speared](entry:spear-and-woomera), out in the open, or else hunted for in hollow logs, or in their burrows' [ref:roth1901]. His most detailed notes come from **Princess Charlotte Bay**, north of Kuku Yalanji country [ref:roth1901]:

1. **Read the tracks.** Hunters there could always tell from the tracks whether a goanna was inside its burrow or not.
2. **Know the burrow's habits.** A goanna goes into one of its burrow holes at sundown and closes it behind it. Next morning it comes out by a different opening, and each day it uses another of the many openings. It may go back in during the hottest part of the day.
3. **Check a log before cutting.** If a hollow log may hold a goanna, push a [lawyer-cane](entry:lawyer-cane) prodder into the hollow, both to feel for the animal and to measure how far in it is.
4. **Cut in** from the outside at the right spot and take it out.
5. In the open, **spear** it (*[damal](word:damal)* 'to spear').

For **cooking**, the simplest way was to lay the meat on and in the hot ashes [ref:roth1901] (*[dindal](word:dindal)* 'to roast on coals') [ref:hershberger1982]. Larger amounts could go in the Bloomfield stone **[earth oven](entry:earth-oven)** (*[kurrma](word:kurrma)*): stones heated in a fire, a hole dug where the fire was, [ginger](entry:wild-ginger) leaves underneath, meat with hot stones and ashes packed in, then leaves or [tea-tree bark](entry:paperbark) and earth on top [ref:roth1901] [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: Safety
sections.body:
**Goannas bite.** A startled lace monitor will usually run up the nearest tree [ref:wtma-monitors], so give a goanna room to get away and never grab one. Bites bleed badly. Monitor-lizard saliva contains toxins, and 'bite victims of varanid lizards often report persistent bleeding exceeding that expected for the mechanical damage of the bite'. Lace monitor toxin has been shown to stop blood platelets clumping [ref:dobson2019]. Clean any goanna bite well and get medical help for deep wounds.

**Cane toads.** In the tropics goannas can be poisoned by eating cane toads [ref:nesp-sandgoanna]. A goanna found dead or dying for no clear reason should not be eaten.

**Food rules.** Keep the old rule. *[Jadi](word:jadi)*, the sand goanna, is for old people [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: On Country today
sections.body:
Goannas are protected native animals in Queensland, and anyone else needs a licence or permit to take them [ref:qld-nca]. They are under pressure from cane toads in the tropics [ref:nesp-sandgoanna].

Section 211 of the *Native Title Act 1993* protects native title holders who hunt for **personal, domestic or non-commercial communal needs** [ref:alrc-s211].

Native title differs from place to place: see each place below. **Ask the Traditional Owners before you hunt.**

locations.summary: Goannas are common in the Hann's country, and **the one you will meet is the yellow-spotted goanna**. The Atlas of Living Australia holds 54 goanna records, dated 2010 to 2026, in a box of about 90 × 85 km around the middle Hann, Laura and western Rinyirru, and 46 of them are *Varanus panoptes* [ref:ala-hann]. A Possum man of the upper Hann told the Federal Court that he hunts goanna [ref:fca-possum]. This is Possum and Thaypan country, not Kuku Yalanji country.

sections.heading: Which goannas live here
sections.body:
In the 90 × 85 km Atlas box [ref:ala-hann]:

- **Yellow-spotted goanna** (*Varanus panoptes*): 46 records.
- **Spotted tree monitor** (*V. scalaris*): 3.
- **Mertens' water monitor** (*V. mertensi*): 2.
- **Lace monitor** (*V. varius*): 1.
- Not identified to species: 2.

The lace monitor, the big forest goanna of the coast, is barely recorded here. The Kuku Thaypan Elders name the yellow-spotted goanna and the sand goanna (*V. gouldii*) among the animals of their country [ref:standley2019].

sections.heading: Its year here
sections.body: In the Kuku Thaypan Elders' calendar, the wattles flowering after the wet are a sign: wattle is 'an indicator for timing of when fish, turtle and goanna are fat' [ref:standley2019]. The calendar puts fat goanna in the same season as the wetlands beginning to dry out and the first early burns [ref:standley2019].

sections.heading: How people hunted them here
sections.body:
A Possum man of the upper Hann described 'hunting pigs, kangaroos, goanna, porcupine, and plain turkeys' on his country [ref:fca-possum].

Roth's most detailed goanna-hunting notes come from **Princess Charlotte Bay**, the coast the Hann runs down to: reading the tracks to tell whether a goanna is in its burrow, and using a [lawyer-cane](entry:lawyer-cane) prodder to find it in a hollow log [ref:roth1901]. They are under 'How they were hunted and cooked' above.

On the **upper Normanby**, boys played 'Iguanas'. One boy half-lay on the ground with his forearm dug into the sand up to the elbow and stuck a finger out here and there, and his mates tried to hit it with a stick [ref:roth1902].

Roth also wrote down goanna stories from the Koko-warra and Koko-rarmul of Princess Charlotte Bay [ref:roth1903]. They belong to their custodians and are not retold here.

sections.heading: On country today
sections.body: The upper Hann is the Possum People's country and the middle and lower Hann are Thaypan country. Their November 2023 determinations recognise rights to hunt on the land [ref:fca-possum] [ref:fca-thaypan]. Downstream, the Traditional Owners of Rinyirru (Lakefield) National Park are the Lama Lama and Kuku Thaypan peoples [ref:qpws-rinyirru-culture]. For anyone else, goannas are protected animals [ref:qld-nca].

sections.heading: Language
sections.body: In Awu Alaya (Kuku Thaypan), the yellow-spotted goanna is **Nhye mulpa** and the sand goanna **Nhye chulpa**, in the spelling of the Elders' fire research project [ref:standley2019]. These are not Kuku Yalanji words.

locations.summary: The dry open woodland and sandy creek beds of the upper Mitchell are goanna country, and the old honey-hunters of the Palmer used goanna fat.

sections.heading: Where they live here
sections.body: The dry open woodland, sandy creek beds and river flats of the Mitchell River country around Mt Carbine and [Karma Waters](place:karma-waters) are goanna country. The Atlas of Living Australia holds records of lace monitors and black-headed monitors from the Mitchell River country west of Mt Carbine, and the yellow-spotted goanna has been recorded in the wider area [ref:ala]. Look for goanna tracks and fresh diggings along sandy banks in the warm part of the day.

sections.heading: How people used them here
sections.body: Goanna fat had its own uses. On the middle Palmer River, close to Western Yalanji country, Roth recorded a honey-hunting trick. A [native bee](entry:native-bees) was caught and its body smeared with 'iguana or snake-fat' with a little feather-down stuck on. It was then let go and followed home to its nest [ref:roth1901].

sections.heading: On country today
sections.body:
On Western Yalanji country, around the Palmer and Mitchell rivers north-west of Mt Carbine, the 2013 determinations recognise rights to hunt, fish and gather for personal, domestic and non-commercial communal purposes. Firearms may be used on a pastoral lease only where there are no stock and after giving the lessee notice [ref:brady2013].

**At Karma Waters.** Karma Waters Station falls under the earlier 1998 *Western Yalanji or 'Sunset' Peoples v Pedersen* consent determination, the first consent determination of native title over a pastoral property in Australia [ref:wyac2020] [ref:kw-about]. See the [Karma Waters guide](/dictionaries/kuku_yalanji/country/places/karma-waters) for what it covers, and ask the Traditional Owners and the station before hunting, fishing or gathering.

locations.summary: On the coast the goannas are the forest ones, *kalajarr* and *walkarr*, the dictionary's scrub goannas [ref:hershberger1982]. The lace monitor, probably one or both of them, is the big monitor of the Wet Tropics [ref:wtma-monitors].

sections.heading: Where they live here
sections.body: Kalajarr and walkarr, the dictionary's 'scrub' goannas, are rainforest and forest animals of Eastern Kuku Yalanji country [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: On country today
sections.body: The 2007 Eastern Kuku Yalanji determination recognises rights to hunt animals but not for trade or commerce [ref:walker2007]. In 2021 the Daintree, Ngalba Bulal, Kalkajaka and Hope Islands national parks were handed back to Eastern Kuku Yalanji and are jointly managed with the Queensland Government [ref:handback2021]. Permission to come onto country belongs to the Traditional Owners [ref:walker2007]. Visitors should ask first.
